God calls Jeremiah: "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you" (1:5). God knows and calls us before we are born.
"They have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and dug broken cisterns" (2:13). Jesus is the fountain of living water.
"Return, faithless children, for I am merciful" (3:12). God keeps inviting his people home.
"Break up your fallow ground" (4:3). Under the old covenant, judgement for unfaithfulness; God longed for a changed heart.
Search Jerusalem for one person who acts justly. God wanted truth and faithfulness, not empty religion.
"Ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is, and walk in it, and you will find rest for your souls" (6:16). Jesus offers that rest.
The temple sermon: do not trust in "the temple of the Lord" while living unjustly. Religion is not a substitute for a relationship with God.
"Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there?" (8:22). Jesus is the healer of his people.
"Let him who boasts boast in this: that he understands and knows me, that I am the Lord who practises steadfast love" (9:24).
Idols are like scarecrows in a cucumber field; the Lord is the true and living God.
The broken covenant. Israel failed to keep the old covenant, preparing the way for the new.
Jeremiah asks why the wicked prosper. "If you have run with footmen and they wearied you…" God strengthens us for the journey.
The ruined linen belt: pride ruins what God meant for glory. God wanted his people to cling to him.
Drought, and false prophets saying all is well. "Though our iniquities testify against us, act, O Lord, for your name's sake" (14:7).
Jeremiah is discouraged, and God says "If you return, I will restore you… I am with you to save you" (15:19-20).
God will bring his people back from all the lands. Hope beyond judgement.
"Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord… like a tree planted by the water" (17:7-8). "The heart is deceitful" (17:9): we needed the new heart God promised.
The potter and the clay: God can reshape a marred vessel. He does not discard us; he remakes us.
The broken jar. Under the old covenant judgement came for idolatry. In Christ, broken lives are made new.
Jeremiah is beaten and complains, yet God's word is like fire in his bones (20:9). The Lord is with him as a mighty warrior.
Jerusalem will fall to Babylon. God set before them the way of life and death.
Warnings to the kings of Judah to do justice. To know God is to defend the poor (22:16).
"I will raise up for David a righteous Branch… The Lord our Righteousness" (23:5-6). Jesus is our righteousness.
Good figs and bad figs. "I will give them a heart to know that I am the Lord" (24:7). God gives the heart we cannot produce.
Seventy years of exile foretold. God sets limits on hardship; restoration has a date.
Jeremiah is threatened with death for prophesying, but is protected. God protects his messengers.
Jeremiah wears a yoke and tells nations to serve Babylon. God's plans are wiser than ours.
Hananiah breaks the wooden yoke with a false promise. True hope rests on God's actual word.
"I know the plans I have for you… plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope" (29:11). You will seek me and find me.
God will restore the fortunes of his people: "I will restore health to you and heal your wounds" (30:17).
"I have loved you with an everlasting love" (31:3). The new covenant: "I will put my law within them… and remember their sin no more" (31:31-34). Fulfilled in Jesus (Hebrews 8).
Jeremiah buys a field during the siege as a sign of hope. "Nothing is too hard for you" (32:17). God promises an everlasting covenant.
"Call to me and I will answer you, and tell you great and hidden things" (33:3). David's Branch will reign; God's covenant cannot be broken.
The people break their promise to free their slaves. Human promises fail; God's promises stand.
The Rechabites' faithfulness to their father. God longs for his people to listen to him.
King Jehoiakim burns Jeremiah's scroll, but God's word is rewritten. God's word cannot be destroyed.
Jeremiah is imprisoned. Even in prison, God's word remains true.
Jeremiah is thrown into a muddy cistern and rescued by Ebed-melech. God sends help in the pit.
Jerusalem falls, but Ebed-melech is saved "because you have trusted in me" (39:18).
Jeremiah is freed and chooses to stay with the poor in the land. God cares for the remnant.
Gedaliah is murdered. Violence and fear cause chaos without God's leadership.
The remnant asks for God's guidance but already intends to go to Egypt. Asking God is only meaningful if we trust his answer.
They go to Egypt anyway. Fear leads people away from God's protection.
The exiles in Egypt worship the queen of heaven. Old habits of idolatry cannot save.
God's word to Baruch: "I will give you your life as a prize" (45:5). God keeps his servants.
Egypt will be defeated. "Fear not, O Jacob my servant… for I am with you" (46:27-28).
The Philistines will fall. Nations rise and fall under God's hand.
Moab's pride is judged, but God will restore Moab's fortunes in the latter days (48:47). God's mercy reaches even enemy nations.
Judgement on many nations, with promises of restoration for Ammon and Elam. God's heart is ultimately to restore.
Babylon will fall and Israel will return: "Their Redeemer is strong" (50:34).
The fall of Babylon. God's people are told to flee from her; in Christ we are called out of darkness into light.
Jerusalem falls and the temple burns, yet the book ends with King Jehoiachin released and eating at the king's table (52:31-34). A glimpse of grace in exile.
